claims.text: The target material is a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy containing intermetallic phases and a matrix.
The wear and corrosion behaviors of the constituent phases have been individually characterized.
Simultaneous elevated-temperature wear and corrosion cause rapid cyclic formation and rupture of transient oxide films at eutectic phase interfaces.
Exposure of chemically dissimilar phases creates local galvanic couples.
Oxide instability and local galvanic coupling synergistically accelerate both wear and corrosion beyond the sum of their separate effects.
Changing oxygen partial pressure and mechanical load will modulate oxide-film stability and rupture frequency at phase interfaces.
Elevated temperature activates rapid oxide formation and accelerated diffusion at phase boundaries.
Transient oxide films preferentially form and rupture at interfaces between the intermetallic phases and the matrix.
Mechanical rupture of newly formed oxide layers repeatedly exposes phase boundaries.
Potential differences between exposed FCC and intermetallic phases drive local galvanic corrosion.
Local galvanic corrosion further destabilizes the oxide film.
Wear-induced oxide removal and galvanic corrosion interact to accelerate overall degradation.
Simultaneous high-temperature tribocorrosion will produce a higher total degradation rate than isolated wear, isolated corrosion, or a microstructure with smaller phase-potential differences.
Repeated exposure of fresh surface will increase wear.
Stronger local galvanic effects during simultaneous exposure will increase corrosion.
The proposed mechanism requires sustained elevated temperature and simultaneous mechanical and corrosive stresses.
The mechanism may not operate at lower temperatures because oxide films are more stable there.
The mechanism may not operate in single-phase alloys lacking interfacial galvanic couples.
A controlled comparison can be made between the standard multiphase alloy and a modified alloy with minimized phase chemical-potential differences while oxygen partial pressure and load are varied.
The mechanism is falsified if the standard and modified alloys show no significant differences in total degradation, wear, and corrosion, or if simultaneous degradation remains additive.
